title: Spirituality as evolutionary mechanism
content_html:
Spirituality as evolutionary mechanism

The concept of “spiritual” can be understood as an emergent adaptation of the human brain and culture. Humans evolved as hyper-sensitive pattern recognisers (better to see a “spirit in the wind” than miss a predator). This “agency detection” bias predisposed us to interpret unexplained events as intentional or other-than-human. Our brains simulate other minds. Extending this capacity leads to imagining invisible minds - ancestors, gods, spirits. Once humans could remember and re-imagine beyond immediate perception, the unseen world became cognitively “real.” Spirituality arises as an extension of memory and imagination.

Spiritual frameworks provide meaning when cause-effect is unclear (illness, death, natural disaster). Once humans grasped their own mortality, belief in something beyond death helped reduce existential anxiety. Powerful experiences (music, art, nature, altered states) generate a sense of “beyond the self.” Spirituality evolved to interpret and stabilise these states. Shared spiritual beliefs knit groups together - rituals, symbols, myths reinforce cooperation and trust. Engaging in rituals, sacrifices, or pilgrimages showed commitment to the group. Like abstract art, spirituality signals surplus capacity (willingness to invest in the non-material). Religion and spirituality externalised memory into traditions, encoding survival knowledge (e.g., taboos about food safety, rules about social behaviour).

Over millennia, spiritual intuitions crystallised into religions, philosophies, mystical traditions. The “spiritual” shifted from concrete spirits to abstract principles (soul, consciousness, emptiness). Many traditions (Buddhism, Taoism, Indigenous cosmologies) define “spiritual” not as another realm but as the web of relations connecting beings and systems. The spiritual evolved because brains detect agency and patterns beyond the visible, minds remember and imagine realities beyond immediate perception, and groups survive better when bonded by shared symbols and rituals.

Humans need meaning to face mortality and uncertainty, so spirituality is less a separate “thing” than an emergent by-product of memory, imagination, and distributed survival systems - a way of holding the unseen, the relational, and the meaningful together.

Openness to transcendence

Awe arises when people perceive vastness (something much larger than the self) combined with a need for accommodation (our mental models must expand to make sense of it). Originally linked to nature, religion, art, music, politics, awe reduces self-focus, creates a “small self,” and increases receptivity to new ideas. Because awe destabilises ordinary schemas, it opens the mind to transcendent or spiritual interpretations - “something bigger than me.” Awe is seen as a “prototype emotion” that blends perceptual, cognitive, and social elements.

Awe disrupts ordinary self-referential processing → invites openness to new frameworks, including spiritual or transcendent interpretations, and is consistently associated with religious/spiritual experiences, mystical states, and ritual contexts (e.g., music, chanting, natural landscapes). By promoting prosociality and openness to transcendent ideas, awe helped groups cohere and endure, because itr creates a sense of being part of something larger - a distributed whole, not just an individual.

Awe, defined by vastness + schema-change, reduces self-focus. This “small self” leads to increased prosociality (helping, generosity). At the same time, it opens people to transcendence, making them more receptive to spiritual frameworks and shared meaning systems.

Cohesion and division

Spiritual concepts are not only cohesive, however; they can also be divisive. Shared beliefs, rituals, and symbols knit communities together. Common spiritual frameworks enable cooperation across large groups (tribes → nations). Awe, ritual, and transcendence can reduce selfishness and promote generosity within the group.

The same cohesion that unites a group can sharpen boundaries against outsiders. When beliefs are held as sacred, they resist compromise - making disputes more intractable. Spiritual narratives can however be co-opted to justify violence, rally soldiers, or frame wars as cosmic struggles - war can decimate populations and resources. On the surface this looks maladaptive.

At an individual level, believing in transcendent punishment/reward can stabilise cooperation. Groups with stronger cohesion may outcompete others, even through violent conflict. Ideas that maximise survival of the group - even at the cost of individuals - can spread. Once “sacred” frames exist, they can be weaponised by leaders or institutions, tipping spiritual energy toward conflict.

This explains the paradixical nature of spirituality - it is both protective and dangerous. It protects against existential threats (gives meaning, coherence), but it also generates existential threats (wars, persecution). In evolutionary terms, spirituality is like fire: an adaptive innovation that increases survival in some contexts, but is destructive if uncontrolled. Spiritual concepts persist because they dramatically increase in-group cohesion and coordination. But that very cohesion makes out-group conflict more likely, sometimes escalating to war. This is not a “bug” but part of the trade-off of multi-level selection: what strengthens one group may endanger the species as a whole.
